grammar_focus: Habits and tendencies: tend to, be inclined to, keep (on) -ing, will/would, be always -ing
goals: mluvit o pracovním dni, režimu a zvycích přesnými kolokacemi (meet a deadline, work-life balance, wind down…)
vyjadřovat zvyky a sklony strukturami tend to, be inclined to, keep -ing, will/would a be always -ing
zdvořile si stěžovat na otravné zvyky a domluvit se na pravidlech; mluvit o tom, co mám a nemám rád

vocab_core.ex: I find it hard to stick to a routine when I work from home.
It took me years to break the habit of checking my phone in bed.
During lockdown I fell into the habit of skipping breakfast.
She makes a habit of walking to work every day.
My dad is a creature of habit – he has the same breakfast every day.
I'm an early bird, so I do my best work before nine.
As a night owl, she tends to start working at ten in the evening.
I keep hitting the snooze button and then I'm late.
A weekend in the mountains helps me forget the daily grind.

vocab_core.cz: rovnováha mezi prací a osobním životem
vocab_core.ex: Flexible hours have really improved my work-life balance.
Our company offers flexible working hours, so I start at seven.
Half of our team works remotely from different countries.

vocab_core.en: be up to your eyes in work
vocab_core.ipa: bi ʌp tə jɔːr aɪz ɪn wɜːk
vocab_core.ex: Sorry, I can't help – I'm up to my eyes in work.
We worked all weekend to meet the deadline.
He tends to take on extra work and then feels stressed.
The project is running two weeks behind schedule.
Nurses often have to work overtime at weekends.
Let's grab a bite before the meeting.
I usually wind down with a book before bed.
I'm making an effort to go to bed before eleven.
He does the bare minimum and leaves at five on the dot.
However busy she is, she always makes time for her kids.

vocab_ext.ex: I felt stuck in a rut, so I changed jobs.
Our receptionist always goes the extra mile for guests.

blocks.label: 1A Warm-up
blocks.instr: Discuss the questions with your partner.
items: Are you an early bird or a night owl? When do you do your best work?
What does a typical working day look like for you? What do you like and dislike about it?
Which of your daily habits would you like to break? Which would you like to start?
Do you think working remotely improves or damages work-life balance?
What do you do to wind down after a long day?

blocks.label: 1B Core vocabulary
blocks.instr: Read the expressions. Tick (✓) those that are true for you at the moment.

blocks.label: 1C Extension
blocks.instr: Idioms and phrases that make you sound more natural when you talk about work and routines.

blocks.label: 1D Match
blocks.instr: Match the situations (1–8) with the expressions (a–h).
left: She checks her email at 6 a.m. and goes running before work.
The report must be ready by Friday noon and it will be.
He has done exactly the same job in the same way for twelve years and feels bored.
She stays in the office until nine to finish things for a client – nobody asked her to.
He has fourteen projects and no free minute this week.
Every morning I press the button on my alarm clock three times.
After a month in the new job, using the system is automatic for me.
He never does more than he absolutely has to.
right: be up to your eyes in work

blocks.label: 1E Your week
blocks.instr: Describe your typical working week to your partner using at least five expressions from 1B–1C. Your partner listens and then says which expression describes you best and why: I think you're a creature of habit, because…

blocks.label: Review: present simple vs continuous, adverbs of frequency
blocks.html:
Present simplePresent continuous
zvyky, fakta, trvalé stavy
I usually start at eight.		děj právě teď, dočasná situace, vývoj
This month I'm starting at seven.

Příslovce frekvence stojí před plnovýznamovým slovesem, ale za slovesem be a za pomocným slovesem: She often works late. × She is often late. × I have never been late.
Výrazy every day, once a week, from time to time stojí obvykle na konci věty.

items.q: I (usually walk / am usually walking) to work, but this week I (take / 'm taking) the tram.
Our team (grows / is growing) fast – we have three new colleagues this month.
She (is never / never is) late for meetings.
Why (do you wear / are you wearing) a suit today? Have you got an interview?
My boss (doesn't believe / isn't believing) in working from home.
I (hardly ever eat / eat hardly ever) breakfast on weekdays.

blocks.label: 2B Word order
blocks.instr: Put the adverb in the correct place and write the whole sentence.

items.q: I check my email before breakfast. (always)
items.a: I always check my email before breakfast.

items.q: He is in the office on Fridays. (rarely)
items.a: He is rarely in the office on Fridays.

items.q: We have lunch together. (once a week)
items.a: We have lunch together once a week.

items.q: Do you work at weekends? (ever)
items.a: Do you ever work at weekends?

items.q: They have missed a deadline. (never)
items.a: They have never missed a deadline.

blocks.label: 2C Quick check: personalities (L1)
blocks.instr: Use adjectives from Lesson 1 to describe the perfect colleague and the worst colleague (at least four adjectives each). Then compare with your partner: The perfect colleague is reliable and easy-going, and he never…

blocks.label: New grammar: talking about habits and tendencies
blocks.html:
StrukturaVýznamPříklad
tend to + infinitiv
(don't tend to / tend not to)		obvykle, mívat sklonI tend to work better in the morning.
We don't tend to eat out during the week.
be inclined to + infinitivmít sklon (často k něčemu ne úplně dobrému)He's inclined to panic when deadlines get close.
keep (on) + -ingpořád, opakovaně (často otravně)I keep forgetting my password.
will + infinitiv (přítomnost)
would + infinitiv (minulost)		typické, charakteristické chováníShe'll sit at her desk for hours without a break.
As a student I'd study all night before exams.
be always / constantly + -ingopakovaný zvyk, který nás rozčilujeHe's always interrupting people in meetings!

Pozor: would pro minulé zvyky jen u dějů, ne u stavů: ✓ I used to have a long commute. ✗ I would have a long commute.
will/would s důrazem (He WILL leave his cup on my desk!) vyjadřuje kritiku.

blocks.label: 3A Choose
blocks.instr: Choose the best option. Sometimes both are possible – then choose the one that sounds more natural.

items.q: I (tend to / am tending to) get up later at weekends.
My colleague (is always borrowing / always borrows) my stapler without asking – it drives me crazy!
When I was a student, I (would / will) work in a café every summer.
I (keep making / keep to make) the same mistake in my reports.
When I lived in London, I (would have / used to have) a two-hour commute.
Our manager (is inclined to / inclines to) change her mind at the last minute.
People who work remotely (tend not to / don't tend) take enough breaks.
My dad (will / would) always read the newspaper before he talks to anyone in the morning – he still does it.

blocks.label: 3B Rewrite
blocks.instr: Rewrite the sentences using the word in brackets. Keep the meaning.

items.q: I usually feel tired after lunch. (tend)
items.a: I tend to feel tired after lunch.

items.q: He forgets his ID card again and again. (keep)
items.a: He keeps (on) forgetting his ID card.

items.q: As a child, I often hid under the table when guests came. (would)
items.a: As a child, I would hide under the table when guests came.

items.q: She leaves dirty cups in the sink all the time and it annoys me. (always)
items.a: She's always leaving dirty cups in the sink.

items.q: Petr often gets angry when he's tired. (inclined)
items.a: Petr is inclined to get angry when he's tired.

items.q: We don't usually work late on Fridays. (tend)
items.a: We don't tend to work late on Fridays. / We tend not to work late on Fridays.

blocks.label: 3C Reading
blocks.instr: Read the article and decide if the sentences are true (T) or false (F). Then answer the questions.
blocks.title: Why we are all creatures of habit
paras: Think about what you did this morning. You probably got up at about the same time as yesterday, went to the bathroom, made a coffee in the same mug and checked the same apps on your phone. According to researchers at Duke University, around 40 percent of what we do every day is not the result of a decision at all – it is a habit.

Habits are the brain's way of saving energy. When we repeat an action in the same situation, the brain links the situation (the "cue") with the action and the reward that follows. After enough repetitions, we no longer need to think. That is why experienced drivers can change gear while having a conversation, and why many of us keep reaching for our phones even when we have nothing to check.

The problem is that the brain does not distinguish between good and bad habits. Office workers, for example, tend to fall into the habit of eating lunch at their desks. They believe they are saving time, but studies show that people who take a proper break are inclined to be more productive in the afternoon. Similarly, people who hit the snooze button every morning will often feel more tired, not less, because their sleep is interrupted again and again.

So how can we break a bad habit? Psychologists say that simply trying harder rarely works. A more effective strategy is to change the cue. If you keep eating biscuits at four o'clock, don't buy them – or replace them with fruit on your desk. If you want to start running, put your trainers next to the bed. Small changes in the environment make the new behaviour easier than the old one.

Building a new habit also takes longer than most people think. A well-known study from University College London found that it took participants on average 66 days – not the famous 21 – before a new behaviour, such as drinking a glass of water after breakfast, became automatic. The good news is that missing one day did not ruin the process. In other words, you don't need to be perfect. You just need to keep going until the new habit becomes second nature.

tf.q: According to the article, almost half of our daily actions are habits.
Habits make the brain work harder.
People who eat lunch at their desks are usually more productive.
Using the snooze button can make people feel more tired.
Psychologists recommend trying harder as the best way to break a habit.
In the UCL study, missing one day stopped the new habit from forming.

open.q: Find four examples of structures for talking about habits (tend to, keep -ing, will…) in the text.
open.a: tend to fall into, are inclined to be, will often feel, keep reaching / keep eating, keep going.

open.q: Which strategy from paragraph 4 could work for one of your own habits? Discuss with your partner.

blocks.label: 3D Listening
blocks.instr: Listen to Jana and Mark, two colleagues, talking during a coffee break (track L02). Answer the questions. If you don't have the audio, one of you reads the transcript from the key.

items.q: Why is Mark tired today?
options: He worked late on a report.
His neighbour's dog woke him up.

items.q: What does Jana say about herself?
options: She can't stick to any routine.

items.q: What annoys Mark about their new colleague?
options: He keeps interrupting people in meetings.

items.q: How did Jana's working life change when the company introduced flexible hours?
items.a: She starts at seven and finishes at three, so she can pick up her kids / she has a better work-life balance.

items.q: What does Mark tend to do when he's up to his eyes in work?
items.a: He skips lunch / grabs a sandwich at his desk and then feels exhausted.

items.q: What do they decide to do at the end?
items.a: To go for a proper lunch together on Friday (and not talk about work).

blocks.label: 3E Make or do?
blocks.instr: Complete the sentences with the correct form of make or do.

items.q: I'm really trying to ______ an effort to leave the office on time.
He just ______ the bare minimum and never volunteers for anything.
Could you ______ me a favour and send this file to the client?
She ______ a habit of reading for twenty minutes before bed.
We need to ______ some research before we ______ a decision.
However busy you are, you should ______ time for your family.
I'm ______ overtime this week to finish the project.
Our new intern is ______ great progress.

blocks.label: 3F Find the mistake
blocks.instr: Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.

items.q: I'm tending to drink too much coffee at work.
items.a: I tend to drink too much coffee at work.

items.q: He keeps to forget his keys.
When I was young, I would live in a small village.
items.a: When I was young, I used to live in a small village.

items.q: She always is complaining about her boss.
items.a: She is always complaining about her boss.

items.q: We didn't meet the deadline because we did a lot of mistakes.
items.a: We didn't meet the deadline because we made a lot of mistakes.

items.q: I'm up to my eye in work this week.
items.a: I'm up to my eyes in work this week.

blocks.label: 3G Role-play: annoying habits
blocks.instr: You share an office. Each of you has some habits that annoy the other one. Use your role card. Complain politely, explain your side and agree on three rules for the office. Use the phrases in the box.

cards.text: You're an early bird: you arrive at 7 and like a quiet office. Your colleague is always phoning friends loudly, keeps leaving dirty cups on the shared desk and will play music without headphones. You tend to eat lunch at your desk – you don't think that's a problem. You want the window open all the time.

You're a night owl: you arrive at 10 and often work late. Your colleague keeps opening the window (you're always cold!), eats smelly food at the desk every day and is constantly reminding you about deadlines. You sometimes call your family during the day – you think it's normal. You like quiet music while you work.

phrases: I don't want to sound rude, but…
It drives me crazy when you…
I see what you mean, but…

blocks.label: 3H Likes and dislikes at work
blocks.instr: Talk about your job (or studies). Use the phrases: I can't stand…, I don't mind…, I'm (not) keen on…, What I like most is…, I'm fed up with…, I really enjoy…
items: What do you like most about your working day? And least?
Which tasks do you tend to put off? Why?
Would you prefer flexible hours or a fixed nine-to-five job? Why?
Do you think it's OK to answer work emails in the evening or at weekends?

blocks.label: 3I Writing (homework): informal email
blocks.instr: Your English-speaking friend is starting a job at your company next month. Write an informal email (120–150 words). Describe a typical working day, the office habits and routines, what people tend to do at lunch, and give two tips. Use at least three structures from 3A–3B (tend to, keep -ing, will, be always -ing…) and five expressions from 1B–1C. Start Hi …, and finish See you soon, …

blocks.label: 4A Memorise
blocks.instr: Learn the expressions below (the app helps you practise them every day). In pairs: one of you reads a Czech meaning, the other says the English expression and makes a sentence about their own routine.

lines.text: Morning, Mark. You look exhausted. Are you OK?
Not really. I pulled an all-nighter. The report for the Brno client was running behind schedule, and the deadline is today at noon.
Oh no. Did you finish it?
Just about. I sent it at five this morning. I'm a night owl, so working late isn't usually a problem, but this time it was too much.
I couldn't do that. I'm an early bird. I tend to fall asleep on the sofa at ten, even when I'm watching something good.
Lucky you. So what time do you start these days?

Seven. Since the company introduced flexible working hours, I start at seven and finish at three. It's completely changed my work-life balance. I can pick up the kids from school and still make time for a run.
That sounds great. I should try it, but I keep hitting the snooze button. Three times every morning.
Old habits die hard. Anyway, how's the new guy? Tomáš, isn't it?
Don't ask. He's nice, but he's always interrupting people in meetings. Yesterday I tried to explain the budget and he kept jumping in with his own ideas.
Maybe he's just nervous. Remember your first month? You'd ask me about the system every five minutes.
Fair point. You showed me the ropes. And now it's second nature.
Exactly. Give him time. By the way, are you eating properly? You look like you're living on coffee.
That's the problem. When I'm up to my eyes in work, I tend to skip lunch. I'll just grab a sandwich at my desk and then by four o'clock I'm completely exhausted.
Classic. You need to wind down a bit. Look, why don't we go for a proper lunch on Friday? The new Thai place by the station.
I'd love that. But only if we don't talk about work.
Deal. No reports, no deadlines, no Tomáš.
Perfect. Now, I really need another coffee.
